## Where this picks up

[Part 3](03-finetuning-lfm2-vl-xray-defects.qmd) LoRA fine-tuned LFM2-VL-450M on real GDXray
casting X-ray images for defect detection + localization. Detection got measurably better.
Localization never worked in any of four configurations — mean IoU exactly **0.00**, every time,
because the fine-tuned model learned to predict the constant box `[0,0,0,0]` regardless of what
was in the image.

Liquid AI released **LFM2.5-VL-3B** this week (Aug 12, 2026) — a 3.1B-parameter successor that,
per their release notes, specifically improves grounding and object detection over the previous
generation. That's a direct, testable claim against exactly the gap post 3 found. So: same task,
same dataset, same eval split, same schema — only the model changes. Does the grounding upgrade
actually close it?

Short version: **detection improved again, in the same shape as post 3. Localization still
didn't work — but it failed in a genuinely different, more specific way than the 450M model did.**

## The task (unchanged from post 3)

Same input/output contract as post 3: one X-ray image + fixed prompt, JSON output
`{"defect": bool, "boxes": [[x1,y1,x2,y2], ...]}`, boxes normalized 0-1000 relative to image
width/height, schema-constrained at generation time with
[Outlines](https://github.com/dottxt-ai/outlines). Same `Detection` Pydantic schema, same
`MAX_BOXES=6` cap, same GDXray Castings dataset (87 series, 3,981 images, 714 defect / 3,267
no_defect), same **series-level** train/eval split (3,313 train / 668 eval) — copied directly
from post 3's manifest files, which point at the shared kagglehub image cache, so this is a
byte-identical split, not a re-shuffle. If the numbers move, it's the model, not the data.

## Zero-shot baseline: the opposite failure mode

| | accuracy | precision | recall | mean IoU (of TPs) | localized (IoU>0.3) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LFM2-VL-450M (post 3) | 26.3% | 21.0% | 100% | 0.00 | 0/131 |
| LFM2.5-VL-3B (this post) | 79.9% | 43.5% | 7.6% | 0.02 | 0/10 |

Post 3's 450M zero-shot flagged `defect: true` on 623/668 images (93.3%) — it wasn't reading the
image, it was riding one default answer. LFM2.5-VL-3B does the **opposite**: it flagged only
23/668 images (3.4%) as `defect: true`, catching just 10 of 131 real defects. 79.9% accuracy looks
good until you notice the eval set is 80.4% `no_defect` — that's almost exactly the majority-class
number. Bigger, newer model, same underlying non-engagement with the image, just a different
default answer to hide behind.

When it *does* flag a defect, the box isn't localized — it defaults to something close to the
whole image, or a coarse grid quadrant:

![Zero-shot LFM2.5-VL-3B: true defect (green) is a small region near the top; the predicted box (red) covers nearly the entire image — a "the defect is everywhere" shortcut, not real grounding.](images/lfm25-zeroshot-wholeimage.png)

Mean IoU across the 10 true positives: 0.02. Not meaningfully different from post 3's 0.00.

## LoRA fine-tune

### Config

Same recipe as post 3's *stable* final configuration — no reason to re-discover instabilities
post 3 already diagnosed: rank 16, `lora_alpha=32`, warmup + cosine LR decay (peak `lr=5e-5`, 10%
warmup), class-weighted sampler (train split is 17.6% defect). Target modules
`q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, out_proj, fc1, fc2` — checked against LFM2.5-VL-3B's actual
`named_modules()` before training rather than assumed; they carry over unchanged from the 450M
architecture. 800 steps, quick-eval on an 80-image held-out subset every 100 steps.

### Training

Loss: 1.85 → 0.83 over 800 steps (noisy, generally down — same shape as post 3). Quick-eval recall
on the 80-image subset: 10% → 45%, with the identical oscillation pattern post 3 flagged as a
likely small-effective-batch artifact (a dip to 5% at step 300, mid-training) — not a one-off,
this really does seem to be a property of fine-tuning a VLM on ~580 real defect examples with a
grad-accumulated batch of 4.

### Full eval, 668-image eval set

| | accuracy | precision | recall | mean IoU (of TPs) | localized (IoU>0.3) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Zero-shot | 79.9% | 43.5% | 7.6% | 0.02 | 0/10 |
| LoRA, step 800 (final) | 71.7% | 35.1% | **51.9%** | 0.01 | 0/68 |

**Detection improved, same shape as post 3.** Recall went from single digits to
majority-catching — 7.6% → 51.9% — at the usual cost: precision and accuracy dropped as the
decision boundary got less conservative (126 false positives vs. 13 zero-shot). Genuine signal
the fine-tune worked on the *presence* half of the task, mirroring post 3's finding that detection
is learnable in this budget even when localization isn't.

**Localization still didn't work. But it failed differently than 450M did — and that difference
is the actual finding of this post.**

## I checked what it's actually predicting — again

Post 3's 450M model collapsed completely: every single predicted box, on every image, was the
literal constant `[0,0,0,0]`. Total collapse, zero information content.

LFM2.5-VL-3B's fine-tuned predictions are *not* collapsed. Across the 68 true positives:

- **Box size is close to correct.** Mean predicted box: 64.6×51.0px. Mean true box: 71.4×46.3px.
  The model learned a genuinely reasonable prior over what a defect-sized bounding box looks like
  in this dataset.
- **Box position is essentially uncorrelated with the real defect location.** Mean offset between
  predicted and true box center: (Δx=-58, Δy=+33), with standard deviation (114, 147) on top of
  that — larger than the box itself, on both axes. That's not a small systematic bias correctable
  with a coordinate-frame fix; it's noise.

![Fine-tuned LFM2.5-VL-3B: a correctly-sized box (red), confidently drawn nowhere near the true defect (green). This is representative, not a cherry-picked failure — mean box size is right; mean position error is larger than the box itself.](images/lfm25-finetuned-box-offset.png)

So the model learned **what** a plausible defect region looks like — shape and scale — without
learning **where** to put it. That's a more specific, more informative failure than 450M's
outright collapse to a constant. It suggests the easy part of the coordinate-regression loss (box
size, which correlates loosely with "defect vs. not" and is nearly constant across the dataset) got
learned quickly, while the hard part — conditioning position on the actual pixels in front of it —
never did, in 800 steps on ~580 real examples.

## Does "improved grounding" hold up?

Liquid AI's release notes for LFM2.5-VL-3B specifically call out improved grounding and object
detection over the previous generation. Something in this experiment is consistent with that:
the model didn't collapse to a lazy constant the way 450M did — it produced structurally
sensible, appropriately-sized boxes instead of giving up. That's real, measurable progress on part
of the problem.

It is not evidence that per-image spatial grounding — actually reading where the defect is and
putting the box there — transfers from a few hundred LoRA examples on a 3B model, any more than it
did on a 450M one. Same headline conclusion as post 3, arrived at through a more specific
mechanism: **detection generalizes fast in this budget; per-image localization doesn't, regardless
of model size or claimed grounding improvements.**

## Comparison across both posts

| | zero-shot recall | zero-shot IoU | fine-tuned recall | fine-tuned IoU | fine-tuned failure mode |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LFM2-VL-450M (post 3) | 100% (over-triggers) | 0.00 | 13.7–58.0%¹ | 0.00 | constant `[0,0,0,0]` |
| LFM2.5-VL-3B (this post) | 7.6% (under-triggers) | 0.02 | 51.9% | 0.01 | plausible size, random position |

¹ unstable across checkpoints — see post 3's step-by-step table.

Two models, ~7x apart in parameter count, released roughly a year apart, arrived at the same
localization ceiling from two different directions. That consistency is itself informative: this
doesn't look like a 450M-specific limitation that a bigger model fixes for free — it looks like a
property of fine-tuning a generalist VLM on a few hundred grounding examples through pure
next-token prediction, independent of scale in this range.

## What's next

Post 3 proposed splitting the job: a dedicated segmentation/prompted-detection model for
candidate regions, handed to the VLM for reasoning, instead of asking one small model to learn
"what" and "where" end-to-end. Nothing here changes that recommendation — if anything, seeing the
same ceiling hold at 3B strengthens it. I still haven't tried that combination; it's next.
Separately, I intentionally scoped LoRA-only for this post (121GB unified memory on the GB10 made
QLoRA's 4-bit quantization unnecessary here) — a full fine-tune, unlocking every parameter instead
of ~0.38% of them, is the other open experiment worth running before concluding localization is
out of reach for a model this size.
